title: The Woman in This Portrait Would Not Paint Again for Thirteen Years
standfirst: David Bomberg's 1932 portrait shows his partner Lilian Holt four years into a silence about her own painting that would run to 1945. It also shows the outcome of a war that had already cost him his early aesthetic and a friend — and it sits inside a paper record so contradictory that even Bomberg's own circle cannot agree on when Holt arrived, what she was owed, or who was really running things.

sections.heading: The Woman in This Portrait Would Not Paint Again for Thirteen Years
sections.body:
Lilian Holt trained at Putney Art School in 1913 and 1914, served in the Women's Land Army during the First World War, then worked the Post Office and Prudential before a spell at Regent Street Polytechnic in 1922. None of that is visible in the paint. What the canvas doesn't tell you is that the woman in it had a training and a vocation of her own, and had already been stopped from using it once.

In 1924 she married the art and antiques dealer Jacob Mendelson. [Wikipedia's account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilian_Holt) is blunt about what followed: "Mendelson reportedly forbade Holt to paint," though the marriage did let her handle and study work by Walter Sickert, Jacob Epstein, Jacob Kramer and, as it happened, David Bomberg, whom she had first met the year before. She divorced Mendelson in 1928 and took up with Bomberg the same year. The prohibition lifted. She did not use the freedom. The same source states it flatly: "Holt did not resume painting until 1945, focusing instead on supporting Bomberg's career." This portrait was made in 1932 — four years into that arrangement, thirteen years before the end of it, and nine years before she and Bomberg were legally married at all, in 1941.

sections.heading: A Sentence About Poverty That Nobody Footnoted
sections.body: [Wikipedia's entry on Bomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bomberg) closes his life with a hard sentence: "Having lived for years on the earnings of his second wife, fellow artist Lilian Holt, and remittances from his sister Kitty, he died in absolute poverty." It is the only sentence in either article that credits her with earning anything, and it carries no citation at all, in an entry that footnotes far smaller claims to the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography. Set beside her own page's flat statement that she did not paint professionally between 1928 and 1945, it does not resolve into one coherent story. Perhaps "earnings" means something other than picture sales. The record does not say, on either page, and neither page reads as though it was written with the other in mind.

sections.heading: The Prize He Won for Drawing a Friend Who Would Not Survive the War
sections.body:
At the Slade in 1911, Bomberg won the Henry Tonks Prize for a pencil drawing of a fellow student, the poet Isaac Rosenberg, part of a cohort Tonks himself later called the school's second "crisis of brilliance." Two years on, Bomberg was expelled for "the radicalism of his approach," a verdict his 1914 solo show at the Chenil Gallery did nothing to soften: [The Mud Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mud_Bath) hung on an outside wall wrapped in Union flags, and it caused, by one account, "the horses drawing the 29 bus... to shy at it as they came round the corner of King's Road." The catalogue carried his own manifesto: "I look upon Nature while I live in a steel city," and, "I APPEAL to a Sense of Form ... My object is the construction of Pure Form. I reject everything in painting that is not Pure Form."

Then came the war. Rosenberg was killed in 1918; so was Bomberg's brother, and his early supporter T. E. Hulme. The losses, in his biographers' words, "permanently destroyed his faith in the aesthetics of the machine age" — the very faith The Mud Bath had been built on. His first version of a commissioned war painting, Sappers at Work, was dismissed by its Canadian sponsors as a "futurist abortion" and replaced with something gentler and more legible. That is the painter who, fourteen years after winning a prize for drawing his dead friend's face, sat his partner down and painted her plainly, in heavy brushstrokes and warm colour, with none of the steel city left in it. Unlike most of the labels this corpus hands out after the fact, "Expressionism" on this one was not a filing error. It was earned, the hard way.

sections.heading: Whose Group Was It? Even the Founders Cannot Agree
sections.body:
In 1945, at Bomberg's own urging, Holt picked up painting again, the same year he began teaching evening classes at Borough Polytechnic. What happened next depends entirely on who is telling it.

By one account, recorded years later by fellow member Leslie Marr in the [Borough Road Collection Archive](https://theresa-kneppers-jf2w.squarespace.com/blog/2017/10/6/leslie-marr-on-the-formation-of-the-borough-group), four of Bomberg's students — Cliff Holden, Dorothy Mead, Edna Mann and Peter Richmond — "banded together with the intention of exhibiting, and also promoting Bomberg's work" in 1946, a year before Holt joined at all. Holden later insisted he was the group's first president: "Because I was most active in conceiving and fostering the group, Bomberg proposed that I should be first President." Two years on, Bomberg called a meeting and announced he would "assume the presidency and would include his own work in future exhibitions," a move Holden and Mead resisted specifically because it meant "bringing in his family, and people that even he thought amateurs."

Holt's own account of the same eighteen months, [preserved in the same archive](https://theresa-kneppers-jf2w.squarespace.com/blog/2017/10/6/lillian-bomberg-on-the-founding-of-the-borough-group), does not just omit a rival president. It corrects one already in print. In her telling, "a nucleus of three students and myself was formed" from the very start, so that no year passed in which she had not already been there; at first there was "no form, no constitution, no secretary, no Treasurer, and certainly no President, as incorrectly published in the Art News and Review"; and "the first President was David Bomberg, and he was elected in 1947 when the group was properly formed." Two people who were both in the room cannot agree on who founded the group, when she joined it, or who ran it first — and one of them is rebutting a magazine.

sections.heading: The Retrospective Came Decades Late, and Not for Him
sections.body:
In 1954 the couple moved to [Ronda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronda), in Andalusia, where Bomberg kept painting the town's gorge and cliffs until his health gave out. He collapsed there in 1957 and died soon after in London — the once-expelled Slade radical, the man who had thought he'd found Pure Form in a steel city forty years earlier, dying, in his own Wikipedia entry's words, "in absolute poverty."

Holt outlived him by twenty-six years and spent a good many of them travelling to paint — Mexico, Basutoland, Andalusia, Yugoslavia, Morocco, Turkey, Iceland — while also working to protect and promote her late husband's reputation. Her first solo exhibition, at the Ben Uri Gallery, did not happen until 1980, when she was eighty-two. In 2023, forty years after her own death, her work was included in [Action, Gesture, Paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilian_Holt), the Whitechapel Gallery's survey of women and global abstraction between 1940 and 1970 — as far as the record shows, the first time Holt was hung as one name among a movement of painters, rather than filed as the wife in someone else's.
